content.text: {"primary_meaning":"Jacob most commonly signifies Israel: the covenant patriarch whose renamed identity becomes the name and representative embodiment of the people descended from him. Thus biblical references to “Jacob” often denote the nation or covenant people collectively.","primary_basis":["Genesis 28:10–15 — God gives Jacob the Abrahamic covenant promises of land, offspring, and blessing.","Genesis 32:24–30 — after wrestling with God, Jacob is renamed Israel.","Genesis 35:9–12 — the renaming is reaffirmed alongside covenant promises concerning a nation and kings.","Genesis 49:1–28 — Jacob’s sons are presented as the ancestral heads of Israel’s tribes.","Psalm 14:7; 24:6; 46:7,11 — “Jacob” functions as a collective designation for God’s people.","Isaiah 41:8–14; 43:1–7 — “Jacob” and “Israel” are parallel names for the chosen covenant people.","Jeremiah 30:7–10,18 — Jacob denotes the nation in distress and restoration.","Hosea 12:2–6 — the patriarch’s history is applied representatively to the nation.","Romans 9:6–13 — Jacob is associated with Israel, covenant election, and God’s purpose of promise."] ,"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Jacob symbolizes the believer transformed by divine grace: initially self-reliant, deceptive, or grasping, but disciplined through suffering and changed through encounter with God.","basis":["Genesis 25:26–34 — Jacob grasps Esau’s heel and acquires the birthright.","Genesis 27:1–36 — Jacob obtains Isaac’s blessing through deception.","Genesis 28:10–22 — God meets Jacob at Bethel while he is fleeing.","Genesis 29–31 — Jacob undergoes prolonged hardship under Laban.","Genesis 32:24–30 — wrestling, wounding, blessing, and renaming provide the central transformation motif.","Genesis 35:1–15 — Jacob returns to Bethel and renews his allegiance to God."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Jacob represents the elect or recipients of grace, contrasted with Esau, emphasizing divine choice rather than human merit.","basis":["Genesis 25:21–23 — the elder is foretold to serve the younger before their birth.","Malachi 1:2–3 — God’s love for Jacob and rejection of Esau.","Romans 9:10–13 — Paul uses Jacob and Esau in discussing election and God’s purpose."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Jacob’s wrestling with God symbolizes persevering prayer, spiritual struggle, or faith clinging to God for returning to God."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Jacob’s life symbolizes the pilgrim journey of the Christian, including exile, divine protection, discipline, worship, and eventual Christ."],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a settled core identification of Jacob with Israel, grounded both in his renaming and in the Bible’s repeated use of “Jacob” as a collective name for the nation. There is no equally settled consensus on a more detailed allegorical meaning of Jacob’s personality or life; transformation, election, spiritual struggle, and pilgrimage are recurring but context-dependent Christian readings."}
